report:
## The claim: "Soursop cures cancer in humans"

**Bottom line: This is false, or at least unsupported.** No credible scientific body has verified soursop (graviola/Annona muricata) as a cure, treatment, or preventive for cancer in humans.

**What the evidence actually shows:**

- **Lab and animal studies only.** Soursop contains compounds called acetogenins (notably annonacin) that have shown cytotoxic effects against cancer cells in petri dishes and in some rodent studies. This is where claims like "10,000 times more effective than chemo" originate — but that comparison has never been tested in humans and is not an accurate extrapolation from lab data ([Snopes](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/soursop-cancer-cure/)).
- **No human clinical trials demonstrating efficacy.** Major fact-checkers and cancer authorities (PolitiFact, Africa Check, AFP, Wikipedia summarizing Memorial Sloan Kettering and Cancer Research UK) all note there is no reliable clinical evidence soursop treats or cures cancer in people ([PolitiFact](https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2022/sep/27/facebook-posts/fact-checking-claims-tree-fruit-soursop-cures-canc/); [Wikipedia/Soursop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soursop)).
- **Safety concerns.** Annonacin, the main "anticancer" compound, is also neurotoxic. Chronic consumption of soursop and related Annonaceae fruits has been linked to "atypical parkinsonism," a Parkinson's-like neurodegenerative disorder, especially documented in the Caribbean ([Wikipedia/Annonacin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annonacin); PubMed study on Caribbean parkinsonism, pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17017523/).
- **Institutional position.** Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center acknowledges biological activity of soursop compounds but does not endorse it as a treatment; it recommends against relying on it in place of conventional therapy.

**Conclusion:** Soursop is an active area of preliminary lab research, not a proven cancer cure. Relying on it instead of evidence-based treatment could be harmful and delay effective care. Encourage your sister to view soursop as, at best, an unproven supplement — not a substitute for medical treatment — and to discuss any use with an oncologist, given the neurotoxicity risk.
